What is the algebraic definition the Dot Product?

Consider two vectors a and b in an n-dimensional space a=⟨a1​,a2​,…,an​⟩, b=⟨b1​,b2​,…,bn​⟩.

The Dot Product of a⋅b is computed as the sum of the products of the corresponding components:

a⋅b=a1​b1​+a2​b2​+…+an​bn​=i=1∑n​ai​bi​

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

What is the geometric definition the Dot Product?

Consider two vectors a and b in an n-dimensional space a=⟨a1​,a2​,…,an​⟩, b=⟨b1​,b2​,…,bn​⟩.

The Dot Product of a⋅b is defined in terms of the magnitudes (lengths) of the vectors and the angle between them:

a⋅b=∥a∥∥b∥cosθ

where

  • ∥a∥ is the magnitude (length) of vector a,
  • ∥a∥ is the magnitude (length) of vector b, and
  • θ is the angle between the two vectors.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

What is the algebraic definition the Cross Product?

Consider two vectors a and b in the 3-dimensional space a=⟨a1​,a2​,a3​⟩, b=⟨b1​,b2​,b3​⟩.

The Cross Product of a×b is the determinant

a×b=​ia1​b1​​ja2​b2​​ka3​b3​​​

which expands to

a×b=(a2​b3​−a3​b2​)i−(a1​b3​−a3​b1​)j+(a1​b2​−a2​b1​)k

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

What is the geometric definition the Cross Product?

Consider two vectors a and b in the 3-dimensional space a=⟨a1​,a2​,a3​⟩, b=⟨b1​,b2​,b3​⟩.

The Cross Product a×b is a vector that:

  • is perpendicular to both a and b (so orthogonal to the plane containing them),
  • has magnitude equal to the area of the parallelogram spanned by a and b:∥a×b∥=∥a∥∥b∥sinθ where θ is the angle between a and b, and
  • has direction given by the right-hand rule.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

What is the definition of the Unit Tangent Vector T to a curve r(t)?

The normalized velocity vector,

T(t)=∥r′(t)∥r′(t)​,

where r(t)=⟨x(t),y(t),z(t)⟩ and r′(t)=⟨x′(t),y′(t),z′(t)⟩ is the velocity vector.

Extra

Requires r′(t)=0 (a regular curve), so the direction of motion is defined.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

Give a geometric interpretation of the Unit Tangent Vector T.

T(t) points in the instantaneous direction of travel along the curve — it is tangent to the curve at r(t). Normalizing r′(t) strips out the speed ∥r′(t)∥, so T records direction of motion only.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

What is the definition of the Principal Normal Vector N to a curve r(t)?

The normalized derivative of the Unit Tangent Vector,

N(t)=∥T′(t)∥T′(t)​.

Extra

Requires T′(t)=0, i.e. the curve is not momentarily moving in a straight line.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

Why is the Principal Normal Vector N always perpendicular to T?

Because ∥T(t)∥=1 for all t, so T(t)⋅T(t)=1. Differentiating both sides with the product rule gives

2T(t)⋅T′(t)=0,

so T′(t) is orthogonal to T(t). Since N is a positive scalar multiple of T′, N⊥T as well.

Extra

This is a general fact: the derivative of any vector-valued function of constant magnitude is orthogonal to the function itself.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

Give a geometric interpretation of the Principal Normal Vector N.

N(t) points in the direction the curve is turning toward — the direction T is instantaneously rotating, which is toward the concave (inside) side of the curve.

Extra

T and N together span the osculating plane, the plane that best approximates the curve near r(t).

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

What is the definition of the Binormal Vector B to a curve r(t)?

B(t)=T(t)×N(t).

Extra

Since T and N are orthogonal unit vectors, B is automatically a unit vector too: ∥B∥=∥T∥∥N∥sin(π/2)=1.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

Give a geometric interpretation of the Binormal Vector B.

B(t) is perpendicular to the osculating plane spanned by T and N — it is the normal vector to the plane that locally best fits the curve. How B changes as t varies describes how that plane twists along the curve.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

Why do T,N,B together form a right-handed orthonormal basis of R3 at each point of the curve?

T and N are unit vectors and orthogonal to each other by construction. B=T×N is then automatically a unit vector orthogonal to both: its magnitude is ∥T∥∥N∥sin(π/2)=1, and a cross product is always orthogonal to both of its factors. The ordering T×N=B makes the triple right-handed by the definition of the cross product.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

What is the Osculating Plane to a curve at r(t0​)?

The plane through r(t0​) spanned by T(t0​) and N(t0​), with normal vector B(t0​):

B(t0​)⋅(r−r(t0​))=0.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

Give a geometric interpretation of the Osculating Plane.

It is the plane that best approximates the curve near r(t0​). The quadratic Taylor approximation

r(t0​)+r′(t0​)(t−t0​)+21​r′′(t0​)(t−t0​)2

lies entirely in this plane, since r′ is parallel to T and r′′ lies in the span of T and N. It is the plane containing the circle that best fits (osculates) the curve at that point.

Extra

For a planar curve, the osculating plane is the plane containing the curve, at every point.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

What is the Normal Plane to a curve at r(t0​)?

The plane through r(t0​) spanned by N(t0​) and B(t0​), with normal vector T(t0​):

T(t0​)⋅(r−r(t0​))=0.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

Give a geometric interpretation of the Normal Plane.

It consists of all directions instantaneously perpendicular to the curve's motion at r(t0​) — the cross-sectional plane obtained by slicing the curve perpendicular to its direction of travel, analogous to cutting a wire perpendicular to its length.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

What is the Rectifying Plane to a curve at r(t0​)?

The plane through r(t0​) spanned by T(t0​) and B(t0​), with normal vector N(t0​):

N(t0​)⋅(r−r(t0​))=0.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

Why is the plane spanned by T and B called the Rectifying Plane?

For a unit-speed curve, the curvature vector r′′(s)=κ(s)N(s) points purely along N, which is normal to this plane. So, to second order, all of the curve's bending happens out of the rectifying plane, not within it: the curve's orthogonal projection onto the rectifying plane is locally straight ("rectified"), unlike its projections onto the osculating or normal planes.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

Compare the three TNB planes by which pair of T,N,B spans each and which vector is normal to each.

  • Osculating plane: spanned by T,N; normal B.
  • Normal plane: spanned by N,B; normal T.
  • Rectifying plane: spanned by T,B; normal N.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

Why do N×B=T and B×T=N also hold, given that B=T×N?

For any right-handed orthonormal basis {e1​,e2​,e3​} with e3​=e1​×e2​, the defining relation holds under cyclic permutation of the indices:

e1​×e2​=e3​,e2​×e3​=e1​,e3​×e1​=e2​.

Applying this with (e1​,e2​,e3​)=(T,N,B) gives the two further identities.

Extra

Only cyclic orderings work; reversing any pair flips the sign, e.g. N×T=−B, since the cross product is anticommutative.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

What is a Vector Valued Function (VVF)?

A Vector Valued Function (VVF)is a function where the input is a scalar and the output is a vector.

r:D⊆R→Rn r(t)=(f1​(t),f2​(t),…,fn​(t))

Examples:

r(t)=(cos(t),sin(t)) r(t)=(t,t2,t3)

Related

Vector-Valued Function of Several Variables: F:D⊆Rm→Rn

What is a Function of Several Variables (FSV)?

A Function of Several Variables (FSV) is a function where the input is a vector and the output is a scalar.

f:D⊆Rn→R f(x1​,x2​,…,xn​)

Examples:

f(x,y)=x2+y2 f(x)=∥x∥2

Related

Function of Several Variables: r:D⊆Rn→R

Vector-Valued Function of Several Variables: F:D⊆Rm→Rn

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

What kind of a field does a Function of Several Variables define?

A Function of Several Variables r:D⊆Rn→R defines a Scalar Field.

Related

Function of Several Variables: r:D⊆Rn→R

Vector-Valued Function of Several Variables: F:D⊆Rm→Rn

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

What is a Vector-Valued Function of Several Variables (VVFSV)?

A Vector-Valued Function of Several Variables (VVFSV)is a function where the input is a vector x∈Rm and the output is a vector y∈Rn.

F:D⊆Rm→Rn F(x)=(f1​(x),f2​(x),…,fn​(x)) x=(x1​,x2​,…,xm​)

Examples:

F(x,y)=(x2−y,x+y2) F(x,y,z)=(xy,yz,xz)

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

What kind of a field does a Vector-Valued Function of Several Variables define?

A Vector-Valued Function of Several Variables F:D⊆Rm→Rn defines a Vector Field.

Related

Function of Several Variables: r:D⊆Rn→R

Vector-Valued Function of Several Variables: F:D⊆Rm→Rn

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

What type of quantity is the arc-length element ds, and how is it derived for a curve parametrized by r(t)=(x(t),y(t),z(t))?

ds is a scalar (a nonnegative length). Start from the Pythagorean theorem on an infinitesimal right triangle with legs dx, dy and dz:

ds=dx2+dy2+dz2​.

Substituting the ordinary single-variable differentials dx=x′(t)dt, dy=y′(t)dt and dz=z′(t)dt gives

ds=x′(t)2+y′(t)2+z′(t)2​dt=∣r′(t)∣dt,

i.e. speed times dt.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

What type of quantity is the line element dr, and how is it computed from a parametrization r(t)?

dr is a vector: an infinitesimal displacement along the curve, in the direction of increasing parameter. Keeping the components instead of taking their magnitude,

dr=(dx, dy, dz)=(x′(t),y′(t),z′(t))dt=r′(t)dt,

the velocity vector scaled by dt.

Extra

Its length recovers the scalar element: ∣dr∣=∣r′(t)∣dt=ds.

Type: Basic Math (and reversed card)::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

dr
Tds

Extra

Here T=r′(t)/∣r′(t)∣ is the unit tangent vector. Read this as a type statement: vector dr equals unit vector T times scalar ds — direction and length factored apart.

Type: Basic Math (and reversed card)::Card 2::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

Tds
dr

Extra

Here T=r′(t)/∣r′(t)∣ is the unit tangent vector. Read this as a type statement: vector dr equals unit vector T times scalar ds — direction and length factored apart.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

What type of quantity is the surface-area element dS, and how is it derived for a surface parametrized by r(u,v)?

dS is a scalar (a nonnegative area). Moving u infinitesimally traces the tangent vector ru​du, and moving v traces rv​dv. These two vectors span a parallelogram whose area is the magnitude of their cross product:

dS=∣ru​×rv​∣dudv.

Extra

This is the two-dimensional analogue of ds=∣r′(t)∣dt: one dimension uses the magnitude of a derivative, two dimensions use the magnitude of a cross product of partial derivatives.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

Why is the vector area element dS defined using the full cross product ru​×rv​ instead of just its magnitude?

Because dS is a vector: it must carry not just the infinitesimal area but also a direction, namely the unit normal to the surface. The cross product ru​×rv​ is already perpendicular to the surface, so keeping it whole — rather than reducing it to its magnitude dS — preserves that direction:

dS=(ru​×rv​)dudv.

Extra

The normal direction is what makes "flux through a surface" meaningful — it records which way you're passing through.

Type: Basic Math (and reversed card)::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

dS
ndS

Extra

Here n=(ru​×rv​)/∣ru​×rv​∣ is the unit normal vector. As with dr=Tds, this factors a vector into a unit direction times a scalar magnitude.

Type: Basic Math (and reversed card)::Card 2::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

ndS
dS

Extra

Here n=(ru​×rv​)/∣ru​×rv​∣ is the unit normal vector. As with dr=Tds, this factors a vector into a unit direction times a scalar magnitude.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

How is the volume element dV computed under a change of variables r(u,v,w), and why does it use a determinant rather than a cross product?

dV=​det[ru​  rv​  rw​]​dudvdw.

This is the three-dimensional version of the area construction: the determinant of three tangent vectors gives the (signed) volume of the parallelepiped they span, just as a cross product's magnitude gives the area of a parallelogram spanned by two vectors. dV is a scalar.

Extra

In Cartesian coordinates this reduces to dV=dxdydz.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

What is ∇ formally, and in what sense is treating it as a vector a "type pun"?

∇=(∂x∂​, ∂y∂​, ∂z∂​).

It is a "vector" whose components are differential operators, not numbers — so it isn't literally a vector. But treating it as one is productive: combining it with a field via the three familiar vector products (scalar multiplication, dot product, cross product) generates the gradient, divergence, and curl respectively.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

What are the domain and codomain field types of grad, and why is that forced by the product it uses?

gradf=∇f:scalar field→vector field.

∇ combines with the scalar field f by scalar multiplication, and scalar × vector = vector, so the result is a vector field.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

What are the domain and codomain field types of div, and why is that forced by the product it uses?

divF=∇⋅F:vector field→scalar field.

∇ combines with the vector field F by the dot product, and vector ⋅ vector = scalar, so the result is a scalar field.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

What are the domain and codomain field types of curl, and why is that forced by the product it uses?

curlF=∇×F:vector field→vector field.

∇ combines with the vector field F by the cross product, and vector × vector = vector, so the result is a vector field.

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

with subscripts denoting partial derivatives.

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

What does the divergence of a vector field measure, and what does its sign tell you at a point?

Divergence measures net outflow per unit volume at a point. A positive value means the point behaves like a source (more flux leaving than entering a small neighborhood); a negative value means it behaves like a sink.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

What does the curl of a vector field measure, and what does its direction represent?

Curl measures the local rotation of the field. Its direction is the axis about which the field locally rotates (by the right-hand rule), and its magnitude reflects the strength of that rotation.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

Why is curl, as usually written, specific to R3, while gradient and divergence make sense in any Rn?

Gradient and divergence are built only from partial derivatives and a dot product, both of which make sense in any dimension. Curl is built from a cross product, ∇×F, and the cross product as an operation returning a vector in the same space is specific to R3.

Extra

In R2 one instead uses the scalar curl Qx​−Py​, the k-component of the R3 curl when F=(P,Q,0) doesn't depend on z. This is exactly the integrand appearing in Green's theorem.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

Why is ∫C​fds guaranteed to be a scalar, and how do you rewrite it as an ordinary integral over t?

f evaluated along the curve is a scalar, and ds is a scalar, so the integrand fds is scalar × scalar. Substituting ds=∣r′(t)∣dt and evaluating f at the moving point r(t),

∫C​fds=∫ab​f(r(t))∣r′(t)∣dt,

an ordinary single-variable integral.

Extra

Example: the mass of a wire with linear density f.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

Why is ∫C​F⋅dr a scalar even though both F and dr are vectors, and how do you rewrite it as an ordinary integral over t?

The dot product collapses the two vectors into a scalar before integration. Substituting dr=r′(t)dt,

∫C​F⋅dr=∫ab​F(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt,

an ordinary single-variable integral of a scalar function of t.

Extra

This is the work done by force field F along C.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

How does the work integral ∫C​F⋅dr relate to the scalar line integral of a component of F?

Using dr=Tds,

∫C​F⋅dr=∫C​(F⋅T)ds,

so the work integral is exactly the scalar line integral of the tangential component F⋅T — a scalar field — along C.

Extra

In components, with F=(P,Q,R), this is often written ∫C​Pdx+Qdy+Rdz, the dot product F⋅dr spelled out term by term.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

Why is ∬S​fdS a scalar, and how do you rewrite it as an ordinary double integral?

f is a scalar and dS is a scalar, so the integrand is scalar × scalar. Substituting dS=∣ru​×rv​∣dudv,

∬S​fdS=∬D​f(r(u,v))∣ru​×rv​∣dudv,

an ordinary double integral over the flat parameter region D.

Extra

Example: the mass of a sheet with surface density f.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

Why is the flux integral ∬S​F⋅dS a scalar, and how do you rewrite it as an ordinary double integral?

The dot product of the vector field F with the vector area element dS collapses to a scalar. Substituting dS=(ru​×rv​)dudv,

∬S​F⋅dS=∬D​F(r(u,v))⋅(ru​×rv​)dudv,

an ordinary double integral of a scalar function of (u,v).

Extra

The flux measures how much of F passes through S.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

How does the flux integral ∬S​F⋅dS relate to the scalar surface integral of a component of F?

Using dS=ndS,

∬S​F⋅dS=∬S​(F⋅n)dS,

so flux is exactly the scalar surface integral of the normal component F⋅n of the field.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

Why does ∭V​fdV have no vector-valued analogue, unlike the line and surface integrals?

A solid region in R3 has no leftover direction to carry: after using all three dimensions to define the region, there is no tangent or normal structure left for a "vector volume element" to point along. So dV is intrinsically scalar, and

∭V​fdV=∭V​fdxdydz

is just three nested ordinary integrals.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

What single pattern do all five vector-calculus integrals share in regards to the result type, and what role does the dot product play in it?

Every one of them evaluates to a scalar. When the field is vector-valued, the dot product with a vector differential element (dr or dS) is exactly what reduces the vector integrand to a scalar before integrating; when the field is already scalar, it's simply paired with a scalar element. Seeing a "⋅" next to a differential is the signal that two vectors are entering and one scalar is leaving.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

State the one-dimensional Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, and describe the general pattern it exemplifies for the vector-calculus integral theorems.

∫ab​f′(x)dx=f(b)−f(a).

The left side integrates a derivative over the 1-dimensional interval [a,b]; the right side evaluates the original function on the 0-dimensional boundary {a,b}, with signs. The general pattern: integrating a derivative of a field over a region equals evaluating the plain field on the region's boundary, whose dimension is exactly one less.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

State the gradient theorem, and identify the type and dimension of each side.

∫C​∇f⋅dr=f(b)−f(a),C:a→b.

The left side is a scalar line integral (1-dimensional) of the vector field ∇f dotted with dr. The right side is the scalar field f evaluated on the 0-dimensional boundary {a,b}, with signs — the derivative ∇ disappears in favor of the bare field f on the boundary.

Extra

Assumes f is continuously differentiable on an open region containing C, and C is piecewise smooth.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

State Green's theorem, and identify the type and dimension of each side.

∮∂D​(Pdx+Qdy)=∬D​(∂x∂Q​−∂y∂P​)dA.

The right side integrates the scalar curl Qx​−Py​ (a scalar field) over the 2-dimensional plane region D. The left side integrates the vector field (P,Q) as a work integral along the 1-dimensional boundary curve ∂D, traversed counterclockwise.

Extra

Assumes P,Q are continuously differentiable on an open region containing D, and D is a bounded region with piecewise-smooth, positively oriented boundary.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

State Stokes' theorem, and explain in what sense Green's theorem is a special case of it.

∬S​(∇×F)⋅dS=∮∂S​F⋅dr.

The left side turns the curl (a vector field) into a scalar flux integrand via ⋅dS, integrated over the 2-dimensional surface S. The right side is F integrated as work along the 1-dimensional boundary curve ∂S. Green's theorem is the special case where S is a flat region in the xy-plane and F=(P,Q,0) has no z-component: then (∇×F)⋅dS reduces to (Qx​−Py​)dA.

Extra

Assumes F is continuously differentiable on an open region containing S, and S is an orientable, piecewise-smooth surface whose boundary orientation is compatible with the chosen surface normal.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

State the divergence theorem, and identify the type and dimension of each side.

∭V​(∇⋅F)dV=∬∂V​F⋅dS.

The left side integrates the divergence (a scalar field) over the 3-dimensional solid V. The right side is F integrated as flux through the 2-dimensional boundary surface ∂V, oriented outward.

Extra

Assumes F is continuously differentiable on an open region containing V, and V is a bounded solid with piecewise-smooth boundary.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

Across the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, the gradient theorem, Green's/Stokes' theorem, and the divergence theorem, what stays the same as the dimension of the region increases from 1 to 3?

In every case, a derivative of a field integrated over an n-dimensional region equals the plain, undifferentiated field integrated over its (n−1)-dimensional boundary. Reading across each equation, the derivative side is always "inside" and the plain field is always "on the boundary," and the dimension always drops by exactly one.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Vector Calculus

Tags: Math Calculus Vectors

In the language of differential forms, how do the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, the gradient theorem, Green's/Stokes' theorem, and the divergence theorem collapse into a single statement?

All four are instances of one identity,

∫Ω​dω=∫∂Ω​ω,

where d is the exterior derivative — a single operator that specializes to the ordinary derivative, gradient, curl, or divergence depending on the type (degree) of the differential form ω. The dimension of Ω determines which specialization appears.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::ODE

Tags: Math Calculus Differential-Equation ODE Theory

What is the order of an ordinary differential equation?

The order of the highest derivative in the equation.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::ODE

Tags: Math Calculus Differential-Equation ODE Theory

What is the degree of an ordinary differential equation, and how does it differ from the order?

The order is which derivative is highest. The degree is the power to which that highest-order derivative is raised, once the equation is written as a polynomial in the derivatives (no fractional powers, roots, or transcendental functions of the derivatives).

For example, (y′′)3+xy′−y=0 has order 2 and degree 3.

Extra

Degree is undefined if the equation is not polynomial in its derivatives, e.g. sin(y′)+y=0 or ey′′=x.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::ODE

Tags: Math Calculus Differential-Equation ODE Theory

What is an autonomous ordinary differential equation?

An autonomous ordinary differential equation is an equation where the independent variable does not explicitly appear in the equation.

An autonomous ordinary differential equation can be expressed in the form:

dxdy​=f(y)

where f(y) is a function that depends only on the dependent variable y.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::ODE

Tags: Math Calculus Differential-Equation ODE Theory

What is a separable ordinary differential equation?

A first-order ODE is separable if it can be written as

dxdy​=h(x)g(y)

where h(x) is a function of x alone and g(y) is a function of y alone.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::ODE

Tags: Math Calculus Differential-Equation ODE Theory

What is a linear ordinary differential equation?

An n-th order ODE is linear if it can be written as

an​(x)y(n)+an−1​(x)y(n−1)+⋯+a1​(x)y′+a0​(x)y=g(x)

where the coefficients a0​(x),…,an​(x) and g(x) depend only on x, not on y or its derivatives. The dependent variable y and every derivative of it appear to the first power and are not multiplied together or passed through a nonlinear function (e.g. no y2, yy′, or sin(y)).

Extra

If g(x)=0 the equation is called homogeneous (linear); otherwise it is nonhomogeneous. This is a different use of "homogeneous" than the homogeneous (degree-zero) first-order ODE dxdy​=f(y/x) — the two notions share a name but are unrelated classifications.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::ODE

Tags: Math Calculus Differential-Equation ODE Theory

What is an exact differential equation?

A first-order ODE written in differential form

M(x,y)dx+N(x,y)dy=0

is exact if there exists a function ψ(x,y) with ψx​=M and ψy​=N, i.e. the left side is the total differential dψ. Equivalently, if M and N have continuous partial derivatives on a simply connected region, the equation is exact iff

∂y∂M​=∂x∂N​.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::ODE

Tags: Math Calculus Differential-Equation ODE Theory

What is a homogeneous first-order ordinary differential equation?

A first-order ODE dxdy​=f(x,y) is homogeneous if f is homogeneous of degree 0, i.e. f(tx,ty)=f(x,y) for all t=0 in the domain. Equivalently, it can be written as

dxdy​=F(xy​)

for some function F. It is solved via the substitution v=y/x (so y=vx, dxdy​=v+xdxdv​), which turns it into a separable ODE in v and x.

Extra

Not the same "homogeneous" as a homogeneous linear ODE (g(x)=0 in an​(x)y(n)+⋯+a0​(x)y=g(x)) — same word, unrelated classification.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Laplace Transform

Tags: Math Calculus Laplace-Transform Theory

What is the definition of the Laplace transform?

The Laplace transform of a function f(t) is a function F(s) defined as

F(s)=L{f}=∫0∞​e−stf(t)dt

where f(t) is a function of exponential order defined for all t≥0.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Laplace Transform

Tags: Math Calculus Laplace-Transform Theory

What does it mean for f(t) to be piecewise continuous on [0,∞)?

On every finite interval [0,N], f(t) has at most finitely many jump discontinuities, and no infinite discontinuities or oscillatory discontinuities.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Laplace Transform

Tags: Math Calculus Laplace-Transform Theory

What does it mean for f(t) to be of exponential order α?

There exist constants M>0, α, and T≥0 such that

∣f(t)∣≤Meαtfor all t≥T

That is, f(t) does not grow faster than some exponential as t→∞.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Laplace Transform

Tags: Math Calculus Laplace-Transform Theory

Under what sufficient conditions does the Laplace transform of f(t) exist?

If f(t) is

  • piecewise continuous on [0,∞) and
  • of exponential order α,

then

L{f(t)}=F(s)

exists for all s>α.

Extra

These conditions are sufficient, not necessary — some functions violating them still have a Laplace transform.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Laplace Transform

Tags: Math Calculus Laplace-Transform Theory

Why must s>α for F(s)=∫0∞​e−stf(t)dt to converge when f(t) is of exponential order α?

Since ∣f(t)∣≤Meαt, the integrand satisfies

∣e−stf(t)∣≤Me(α−s)t

This decays as t→∞ only when α−s<0, i.e. s>α, which guarantees the integral converges.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Laplace Transform

Tags: Math Calculus Laplace-Transform Theory

Why does f(t)=et2 have no Laplace transform?

et2 is not of exponential order: for any α,

eαtet2​=et2−αt→∞as t→∞

so no bound Meαt can contain it. Consequently e−stet2→∞ as t→∞ for every s, and

∫0∞​e−stet2dt

diverges for every s.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Laplace Transform

Tags: Math Calculus Laplace-Transform Theory

What is the linearity property of the Laplace transform?

For constants a,b and functions f(t),g(t) with transforms F(s),G(s):

L{af(t)+bg(t)}=aF(s)+bG(s)

This follows directly from the linearity of the integral defining L.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Laplace Transform

Tags: Math Calculus Laplace-Transform Theory

What is the first translation or shifting property of the Laplace transform?

If f(t) has the transform F(s) then

L{ectf(t)}=F(s−c) L−1{F(s−c)}=ectf(t)

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Laplace Transform

Tags: Math Calculus Laplace-Transform Theory

What is the second translation or shifting property of the Laplace transform?

If f(t) has the transform F(s) and c≥0 then

L{f(t−c)u(t−c)}=e−csF(s) L−1{e−csF(s)}=f(t−c)u(t−c)

where u(t−c) is the unit step function, which is defined as

u(t−c)={10​t≥ct<c​

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Laplace Transform

Tags: Math Calculus Laplace-Transform Theory

What is the change of scale property of the Laplace transform?

If f(t) has the transform F(s) and c>0 then

L{f(ct)}=c1​F(cs​) L−1{c1​F(cs​)}=f(ct)

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Laplace Transform

Tags: Math Calculus Laplace-Transform Theory

What is the Laplace transform of the first derivative f′(t)?

L{f′(t)}=sF(s)−f(0)

Extra

Requires f(t) continuous on [0,∞) and of exponential order, and f′(t) piecewise continuous.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Laplace Transform

Tags: Math Calculus Laplace-Transform Theory

What is the Laplace transform of the second derivative f′′(t)?

L{f′′(t)}=s2F(s)−sf(0)−f′(0)

Extra

Requires f(t),f′(t) continuous on [0,∞) and of exponential order, and f′′(t) piecewise continuous.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Laplace Transform

Tags: Math Calculus Laplace-Transform Theory

What is the Laplace transform of the nth derivative f(n)(t)?

L{f(n)(t)}​=snF(s)−sn−1f(0)−sn−2f′(0)−sn−3f′′(0)−⋯−f(n−1)(0)​

Extra

Requires f,f′,…,f(n−1) continuous on [0,∞) and of exponential order, and f(n) piecewise continuous.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Laplace Transform

Tags: Math Calculus Laplace-Transform Theory

What is the effect of multiplying f(t) by tn on its Laplace transform?

L{tnf(t)}=(−1)ndsndn​F(s)

Obtained by differentiating F(s)=∫0∞​e−stf(t)dt under the integral sign n times.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Laplace Transform

Tags: Math Calculus Laplace-Transform Theory

What is the convolution f∗g of two functions?

(f∗g)(t)=∫0t​f(τ)g(t−τ)dτ

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Laplace Transform

Tags: Math Calculus Laplace-Transform Theory

What is the convolution theorem for Laplace transforms?

L{f∗g}=F(s)G(s)

The transform of a convolution is the product of the transforms. This lets you compute the inverse transform of a product F(s)G(s) as the convolution f∗g instead of partial fractions.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Laplace Transform

Tags: Math Calculus Laplace-Transform Theory

What is the initial value theorem for Laplace transforms?

If f and f′ are of exponential order and F(s)=L{f(t)}, then

t→0+lim​f(t)=s→∞lim​sF(s)

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Laplace Transform

Tags: Math Calculus Laplace-Transform Theory

What is the final value theorem for Laplace transforms?

If f and f′ are of exponential order and limt→∞​f(t) exists, then

t→∞lim​f(t)=s→0lim​sF(s)

Extra

This only applies when limt→∞​f(t) actually exists (e.g. all poles of sF(s) lie in the open left half-plane) — otherwise the formal right-hand limit can still exist and give a wrong answer.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Laplace Transform

Tags: Math Calculus Laplace-Transform Theory

What is the Laplace transform of a periodic function f(t) with period T?

L{f(t)}=1−e−sT1​∫0T​e−stf(t)dt

What is the unit step function u(t−c)?

The unit step function (Heaviside function) u(t−c) is defined as

u(t−c)={10​t≥ct<c​

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Laplace Transform

Tags: Math Calculus Laplace-Transform Theory

What is the effect of multiplying by the unit step function u(t−c)?

Let f(t)=0 for all t<0.

  • f(t)u(t−c) with c>0 is f(t) switched on at the point c.
  • f(t−c)u(t−c) with c>0 is f(t) shifted (translated) to the right by the amount c.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

What is the unit impulse function δ(t−c)?

The unit impulse function (Dirac delta function) is defined by

δ(t−c)={∞0​t=ct=c​

It is technically not a function but a generalized function or distribution.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Calculus::Laplace Transform

What is the area under the unit impulse function δ(t−c)?

For c≥0, the unit impulse function has unit area:

∫0∞​δ(t−c)dt=1

What is the shifting or sampling property of the unit impulse function δ(t−c)?

Integrating a function f(t) against δ(t−c) recovers the value of f at c:

∫−∞∞​f(t)δ(t−c)dt=f(c)

What is the derivative of the unit step function?

The derivative of the unit step function (Heaviside function) is the unit impulse function (Dirac delta function):

dtd​u(t)=δ(t)

Tags: Math Linear-Algebra

What is a linear equation?

A linear equation is an algebraic equation in which each term is either a constant or the product of a constant and a single variable. Linear equations can have one or more variables.

The general form of a linear equation in two variables x and y is:

ax+by=c

where a, b, and c are constants, and a and b are not both zero.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Linear Algebra

Tags: Math Linear-Algebra

What is a system of linear equations?

A system of linear equations is a collection of one or more linear equations involving the same set of variables.

For example, the following is a system of two linear equations with two variables x and y:

2x+3y4x−y​=6=5​

The solution to a system of linear equations is the set of values for the variables that satisfy all the equations simultaneously.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Linear Algebra

Tags: Math Linear-Algebra

What is a homogeneous system of linear equations?

A homogeneous system of linear equations is a system in which all of the constant terms are zero.

For example, the following is a homogeneous system of two linear equations with two variables x and y:

2x+3y4x−y​=0=0​

A homogeneous system always has at least one solution, known as the trivial solution, where all variables are equal to zero (e.g., x=0 and y=0).

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Linear Algebra

Tags: Math Linear-Algebra

What is the difference between a inconsistent and an consistent system of linear equations?

A system of linear equations is consistent if there is at least one set of values for the variables that satisfies all the equations simultaneously. In other words, a consistent system has at least one solution.

A system of linear equations is inconsistent if there are no solutions. This occurs when the equations represent parallel lines (in two dimensions) or planes (in three dimensions) that do not intersect.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Linear Algebra

Tags: Math Linear-Algebra

What is the difference between a dependent and an independent system of linear equations?

A system of linear equations is independent if the equations are not multiples of each other, meaning they provide unique information about the variables. An independent system has a unique solution.

A system of linear equations is dependent if at least one equation can be derived from the others, meaning they do not provide unique information about the variables. A dependent system has either infinitely many solutions or no solution.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Linear Algebra

Tags: Math Linear-Algebra Matrix

What is a diagonal matrix?

A diagonal matrix is a square matrix in which all entries outside the main diagonal are zero. The main diagonal runs from the top left to the bottom right of the matrix.

For example, the following is a 3×3 diagonal matrix:

​a11​00​0a22​0​00a33​​​

where a11​, a22​, and a33​ are the diagonal elements.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Linear Algebra

Tags: Math Linear-Algebra Matrix

What is a upper-trianguar matrix?

An upper-triangular matrix is a square matrix in which all entries below the main diagonal are zero. The main diagonal runs from the top left to the bottom right of the matrix.

For example, the following is a 3×3 upper-triangular matrix:

​a11​00​a12​a22​0​a13​a23​a33​​​

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Linear Algebra

Tags: Math Linear-Algebra Matrix

What is a lower-trianguar matrix?

An lower-triangular matrix is a square matrix in which all entries above the main diagonal are zero. The main diagonal runs from the top left to the bottom right of the matrix.

For example, the following is a 3×3 lower-triangular matrix:

​a11​a21​a31​​0a22​a32​​00a33​​​

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Linear Algebra

Tags: Math Linear-Algebra Matrix

What is the identity matrix I?

The identity matrix I is a square matrix in which all the elements of the main diagonal are ones, and all other elements are zeros. The main diagonal runs from the top left to the bottom right of the matrix.

For example, the following is a 3×3 identity matrix:

​100​010​001​​

The identity matrix acts as the multiplicative identity in matrix multiplication, meaning that for any matrix A of compatible size:

AI=IA=A

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Linear Algebra

Tags: Math Linear-Algebra Matrix

What is a symmetric matrix?

A symmetric matrix is a square matrix that is equal to its transpose. In other words, a matrix A is symmetric if:

A=AT

This means that the elements across the main diagonal are mirror images of each other, i.e., aij​=aji​ for all i and j.

For example, the following is a 3×3 symmetric matrix:

​123​245​356​​

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Linear Algebra

Tags: Math Linear-Algebra Matrix

What are the multiplication properties of matrices?

Matrix multiplication follows the distributive law:

A(B±C)(A±B)C​=AB±AC=AC±BC​

Matrix multiplication follows the associative law:

A(BC)=(AB)C

In general, matrix multiplication is not commutative:

AB=BA

Except when multiplying by the identity matrix I:

AI=IA

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Linear Algebra

Tags: Math Linear-Algebra Matrix

Is matrix multiplication distributive?

Yes, matrix multiplication is distributive. For matrices A, B, and C (of compatible sizes), the following properties hold:

A(B±C)(A±B)C​=AB±AC=AC±BC​

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Linear Algebra

Tags: Math Linear-Algebra Matrix

Is matrix multiplication associative?

Yes, matrix multiplication is associative. For matrices A, B, and C (of compatible sizes), the following properties hold:

A(BC)=(AB)C

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Linear Algebra

Tags: Math Linear-Algebra Matrix

Is matrix multiplication commutative?

No, matrix multiplication is not commutative. For any matrices A and B:

AB=BA

Except when multiplying by the identity matrix I:

AI=IA

Deck: Math::Linear Algebra

Tags: Math Linear-Algebra Matrix

What is the inverse of a square matrix?

The inverse of a square matrix A is a square matrix A−1 such that:

A⋅A−1=A−1⋅A=I

where I is the identity matrix of the same size as A.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Linear Algebra

Tags: Math Linear-Algebra Matrix

What are the properties of symmetric matrices?

Suppose that is A symmetric matrix. Then, we have the following properties:

  • −A is symmetric.
  • cA is symmetric for any c=0.
  • Am is symmetric for any positive integer m.
  • A−1 is symmetric for nonsingular A.

If A and B symmetric matrices, we have the following properties:

  • The sum A+B is symmetric.
  • The product A⋅B is not always symmetric.

Finally:

  • A+AT is symmetric for any square matrix A.
  • A⋅AT and AT⋅A is symmetric for any m×n matrix A.

Any diagonal matrix is symmetric.

If A is a symmetric matrix, is Am symmetric?:

Yes, Am is symmetric for a symmetric matrix A and a positive integer m.

Yes, A−1 is symmetric for a nonsingular symmetric matrix A.

If A and B are symmetric matrices, is their sum A+B symmetric?:

Yes, the sum A+B is symmetric for two symmetric matrices A and B.

If A and B are symmetric matrices, is their product A⋅B symmetric?:

No, the product A⋅B is not always symmetric.

The sum A+AT is symmetric for any square n×n matrix A.

What is a singular square matrix?

A square matrix A is singular if its determinant is zero:

det(A)=0

A singular square matrix A cannot be inverted, meaning A−1 does not exist.

When a matrix does not have an inverse?

A matrix A does not have an inverse if:

  • It is not square.
  • It is singular, meaning its determinant is zero det(A)=0.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Linear Algebra

Tags: Math Linear-Algebra Determinant

When the determinant of a matrix is zero?

A square matrix has zero determinant when its rows or columns are linearly dependent - meaning one row (or column) can be written as a linear combination of the others.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Linear Algebra

Tags: Math Linear-Algebra Determinant

What is the geometric interpretation of the absolute determinant value of a matrix?

For a square matrix A, the absolute value of the determinant ∣det(A)∣ is the factor by which the matrix scales n-dimensional volume:

  • ∣det(A)∣=0: the transformation flattens space into a lower dimension (e.g., collapsing area or volume to zero).
  • ∣det(A)∣=1: the transformation preserves area/volume (it may rotate, reflect, or shear, but doesn't scale).
  • ∣det(A)∣>1: volumes are expanded.
  • ∣det(A)∣<1: volumes are contracted.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Linear Algebra

Tags: Math Linear-Algebra Determinant

What is the geometric interpretation of the zero determinant of a matrix?

A determinant is zero whenever the transformation collapses space into a lower dimension.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Linear Algebra

Tags: Math Linear-Algebra Determinant

When the determinant of a triangular matrix is zero?

The determinant of a triangular matrix is zero whenever one of its diagonal entries is zero.

What is the determinant of a 2×2 matrix A?

Given a 2×2 matrix A=[ac​bd​] its determinant is computed as:

det(A)​=​ac​bd​​=ad−bc​

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Linear Algebra

What is the determinant of a 3×3 matrix A?

Given a 3×3 matrix A=​adg​beh​cfi​​ its determinant is computed as:

det(A)​=​adg​beh​cfi​​=a​eh​fi​​−b​dg​fi​​+c​dg​eh​​=a(ei−fh)−b(di−fg)+c(dh−eg)​

It is simply a cofactor expansion along the first row.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Linear Algebra

Tags: Math Linear-Algebra Determinant

What is the minor Mij​ of the entry aij​ in a matrix A?

The minor Mij​ of the entry aij​ in a matrix A is the determinant of the remaining entries when the row and column containing aij​ are removed.

Example:

For the matrix A=​147​258​369​​, the minor M22​ of the entry a22​=5 is computed by removing the second row and second column, resulting in the submatrix [17​39​]:

M22​=​17​39​​

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Linear Algebra

Tags: Math Linear-Algebra Determinant

What is the cofactor Cij​ of the entry aij​ in a matrix A?

The cofactor Cij​ of the entry aij​ is in a matrix A is given by:

Cij​=(−1)i+j⋅Mij​

where Mij​ is the minor of the entry aij​.

Example:

For the matrix A=​147​258​369​​, the cofactor C21​ of the entry a21​=4 is

Cij​​=(−1)2+1⋅M21​=−​28​39​​​

Cofactors are a useful tool in helping us to compute determinants of larger matrices.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Linear Algebra

Tags: Math Linear-Algebra Determinant

How to use the cofactor expansion to compute the determinant of a square matrix A?

The determinant of a square matrix A can be computed using cofactors by expanding along any row or column.

For example, the cofactor expansion across the first row i=1 is:

det(A)​=j=1∑n​a1j​C1j​=a11​C11​+a12​C12​+⋯+a1n​C1n​​

Or, the cofactor expansion across the second column j=2 is:

det(A)​=i=1∑m​ai2​Ci2​=a12​C12​+a22​C22​+⋯+am2​Cm2​​

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Linear Algebra

Tags: Math Linear-Algebra Determinant

What is the Laplace expansion to compute the determinant of a square matrix A?

The Laplace expansion to compute the determinant is the cofactor expansion along any row or column.

What is the inverse of a 2×2 matrix A?

Given a 2×2 matrix A=[ac​bd​], its inverse A−1 is computed as:

A−1=det(A)1​[d−c​−ba​]=ad−bc1​[d−c​−ba​]

What is the affine transformation?

An affine transformation is a function between affine spaces that preserves points, straight lines, and planes, but not necessarily distances or angles. Examples include translation, scaling, rotation, and shearing.

An affine transformation T:R2→R2 is defined as

x=Au+b

where x, u and b are 2×1 column vectors and A is a 2×2 matrix.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Linear Algebra

Tags: Math Linear-Algebra Matrix

What does it mean for an affine transformation to preserve orientation?

Preserving orientation means that the transformation does not flip the space, maintaining the clockwise or counterclockwise arrangement of points.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Linear Algebra

Tags: Math Linear-Algebra Matrix

When an affine transformation preserves orientation?

An affine transformation T preserves orientation if

det(A)>0

and does not preserve orientation if the determinant is negative:

det(A)<0

where the matrix A that represents the linear transformation associated with T.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Linear Algebra

Tags: Math Linear-Algebra Matrix

When an affine transformation is invertible?

An affine transformation T is invertible if and only if the matrix A that represents the linear transformation associated with T is invertible, that is det(A)=0.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Linear Algebra

Tags: Math Linear-Algebra Matrix

What is an eigenvector v of a square matrix A?

Given a matrix A an eigenvector of A is a non-zero vector v such that

Av=λv

for some scalar λ∈R, λ=0. The scalar λ is called the eigenvalue corresponding to the eigenvector v.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Extra

Tags: Math Calculus Center-of-Mass

What is the formula for the moment of a system of particles about the origin?

The moment MO​ of a system of particles about the origin is given by the formula:

MO​=i=1∑n​mi​ri​
  • mi​ is the mass of the i-th particle, and
  • ri​ is the position vector of the i-th particle.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Extra

Tags: Math Calculus Center-of-Mass

What is the formula for the center of mass of a system of particles?

The center of mass R of a system of particles is given by the formula:

R=m1​i=1∑n​mi​ri​

where

  • m=∑i=1n​mi​ is the total mass of the system,
  • mi​ is the mass of the i-th particle, and
  • ri​ is the position vector of the i-th particle.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Extra

Tags: Math Functions Terminology

How are the terms "function" and "mapping" related?

In most elementary mathematics, a mapping is the same kind of object as a function: a rule assigning each input from one set exactly one output in another set.

The word "mapping" often emphasizes movement from one set or space to another:

f:A→B.

Related

Other common synonyms include map, transformation, and operator, though these words often suggest a specific context.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Extra

Tags: Math Functions Terminology

What is the difference between the codomain and the range of a function f:A→B?

The codomain is the declared target set B. The range, or image, is the set of outputs that actually occur:

range(f)={f(a):a∈A}.

So the range is always a subset of the codomain.

Extra

If f:R→R is given by f(x)=x2, then the codomain is R, but the range is [0,∞).

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Extra

Tags: Math Functions Terminology

What does it mean for a mapping T:V→W to be linear?

Assuming V and W are vector spaces over the same field, T is linear if it preserves vector addition and scalar multiplication:

T(u+v)=T(u)+T(v)

and

T(cv)=cT(v)

for all u,v∈V and all scalars c.

Related

Equivalently, a linear map preserves linear combinations:

T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v).

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Extra

Tags: Math Functions Terminology

Why must every linear mapping T:V→W satisfy T(0)=0?

Because linearity gives

T(0)=T(0+0)=T(0)+T(0).

Subtracting T(0) from both sides gives

T(0)=0.

So any mapping that does not send the zero vector to the zero vector cannot be linear.

Extra

This is often the fastest way to see that f(x)=mx+b is not a linear map when b=0, even though its graph is a straight line.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Extra

Tags: Math Functions Terminology

Why can the phrase "linear function" be confusing in calculus and linear algebra?

In elementary calculus, "linear function" often means a function whose graph is a line:

f(x)=mx+b.

In linear algebra, a linear mapping must preserve addition and scalar multiplication, so for f:R→R, it must have the form

f(x)=mx.

The function f(x)=mx+b with b=0 is affine, not linear in the linear algebra sense.

Related

Every linear map R→R has a straight-line graph through the origin, but not every straight-line graph represents a linear map.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Extra

Tags: Math Functions Terminology

Compare a general function, a mapping, and a linear mapping.

  • A general function f:A→B assigns each input in A exactly one output in B.
  • A mapping is usually another word for a function, often used when emphasizing movement between sets or spaces.
  • A linear mapping is a special kind of function between vector spaces that preserves vector addition and scalar multiplication.

The definition of the Arithmetic Mean (AM).

The Arithmetic Mean (AM) of two numbers a and b is given by:

AM=2a+b​

The general formula for n numbers x1​,x2​,…,xn​ is:

AM=nx1​+x2​+…+xn​​=n1​i=1∑n​xi​

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Extra

Tags: Math Algebra Mean

The definition of the Geometric Mean (GM).

The Geometric Mean (GM) of two numbers a and b is given by:

GM=ab​

The general formula for n numbers x1​,x2​,…,xn​ is:

GM=(x1​⋅x2​⋅…⋅xn​)1/n=(i=1∏n​xi​)1/n

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Extra

Tags: Math Algebra Mean

The definition of the Quadratic Mean (QM).

The Quadratic Mean (QM) of two numbers a and b is given by:

QM=2a2+b2​​

This is also known as the Root Mean Square (RMS).

The general formula for n numbers x1​,x2​,…,xn​ is:

QM=nx12​+x22​+…+xn2​​​=n1​i=1∑n​xi2​​

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Extra

Tags: Math Algebra Mean

The definition of the Harmonic Mean (HM).

The Harmonic Mean (HM) of two numbers a and b is given by:

HM=1/a+1/b2​=a+b2ab​

The general formula for n numbers x1​,x2​,…,xn​ is:

HM=x1​1​+x2​1​+…+xn​1​n​=∑i=1n​xi​1​n​

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Extra

Tags: Math Algebra Mean

AM-GM Inequality

2a+b​≥ab​

where AM is the Arithmetic Mean and GM is the Geometric Mean of two non-negative numbers a and b.

Extra

More generally, it is known that the following inequality holds for any set of positive numbers:

QM≥AM≥GM≥HM

where

  • QM is the Quadratic Mean
  • AM is the Arithmetic Mean
  • GM is the Geometric Mean
  • HM is the Harmonic Mean

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Extra

Tags: Math Algebra Mean

What is the general formula for means?

The general formula is the Kolmogorov–Nagumo (Quasi-Arithmetic) Mean:

Mf​(x1​,x2​,…,xn​)​=f−1(n1​i=1∑n​f(xi​))=f−1(nf(x1​)+f(x2​)+…+f(xn​)​)​

where f is any continuous strictly monotone function.

  • If f(x)=x, we get the Arithmetic Mean.
  • If f(x)=lnx, we get the Geometric Mean (requires xi​>0).
  • If f(x)=1/x, we get the Harmonic Mean (requires xi​=0).
  • If f(x)=xp (with p=0), we get the Power Mean, with p=2 being the Quadratic Mean.

So the Quasi-Arithmetic Mean is the most general form that unites all the classical means.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Extra

Tags: Math Logic

Given a hypothesis H and a condition C, define what it means for C to be necessary for H.

C is necessary for H if

H⟹C.

Whenever H holds, C must also hold.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Extra

Tags: Math Logic

Given a hypothesis H and a condition C, define what it means for C to be sufficient for H.

C is sufficient for H if

C⟹H.

Whenever C holds, H must also hold.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Extra

Tags: Math Logic

If C is necessary for H, and C is true, what does that tell us about H?

Nothing definite. Necessity only gives H⟹C, not the reverse implication C⟹H. So C can be true in cases where H is false; knowing C alone does not establish H.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Extra

Tags: Math Logic

If C is necessary for H, and C is false, what does that tell us about H?

H must be false. Since necessity means H⟹C, contraposition gives ¬C⟹¬H. A failed necessary condition rules out the hypothesis.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Extra

Tags: Math Logic

If C is necessary for H, and H is true, what does that tell us about C?

C must be true. Necessity means H⟹C, so every case satisfying H also satisfies C.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Extra

Tags: Math Logic

If C is necessary for H, and H is false, what does that tell us about C?

Nothing definite. From H⟹C, the falsehood of H does not imply either C or ¬C. The necessary condition may be true or false when the hypothesis fails.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Extra

Tags: Math Logic

If C is sufficient for H, and C is true, what does that tell us about H?

H must be true. Sufficiency means C⟹H by definition, so once C is known to be true, modus ponens directly yields H.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Extra

Tags: Math Logic

If C is sufficient for H, and C is false, what does that tell us about H?

Nothing definite. From C⟹H, the falsehood of C does not imply either H or ¬H. The hypothesis may still be true for some other reason.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Extra

Tags: Math Logic

If C is sufficient for H, and H is true, what does that tell us about C?

Nothing definite. From C⟹H, the truth of H does not imply C. A sufficient condition is one way for the hypothesis to hold, not necessarily the only way.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Extra

Tags: Math Logic

If C is sufficient for H, and H is false, what does that tell us about C?

C must be false. Since sufficiency means C⟹H, contraposition gives ¬H⟹¬C. A false hypothesis rules out any sufficient condition for it.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Extra

Tags: Math Logic

What does it mean for C to be both necessary and sufficient for H, and how is this written using implications?

C is necessary and sufficient for H when both H⟹C and C⟹H hold, i.e.

C⟺H.

C and H are then logically equivalent: each is true in exactly the same cases as the other.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Extra

Tags: Math Logic

Is differentiability of f at a necessary, sufficient, both, or neither for continuity of f at a?

Sufficient but not necessary. Differentiability at a implies continuity at a. The converse fails: f(x)=∣x∣ is continuous at 0 but not differentiable there.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Extra

Tags: Math Logic

For a differentiable function f, is f′(a)=0 necessary, sufficient, both, or neither for f to have a local extremum at a?

Necessary but not sufficient. If f has a local extremum at an interior point a where it is differentiable, Fermat's theorem gives f′(a)=0. The converse fails: f(x)=x3 has f′(0)=0 but no extremum at 0.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Extra

Tags: Math Logic

Is an​→0 necessary, sufficient, both, or neither for the series ∑an​ to converge?

Necessary but not sufficient. If ∑an​ converges, the term test forces an​→0. The converse fails: the harmonic series ∑1/n has terms tending to 0 yet diverges.

Type: Basic Math::Card 1::Back

Deck: Math::Extra

Tags: Math Logic

For a square matrix A, is det(A)=0 necessary, sufficient, both, or neither for A being invertible?

Both — necessary and sufficient. A is invertible if and only if det(A)=0.
